historical_record.description: Italian-American growers' and dealers' associations built a wood-frame Colombo Market on the block bounded by Front, Davis, Jackson and Clark streets, the first enclosed wholesale produce market in San Francisco, replacing the open-air street market on Sansome Street.
Michael Perata, a Genoese farmer and commission merchant, ran a vegetable business from stalls 23-24 in the Colombo Market until 1891.
The San Francisco Call predicted the decaying wooden Colombo Market, then sinking into the bay fill, would not survive the year.

The Zeille family, owners of the site, built a $50,000 Italian Renaissance brick market in place of the wooden one and leased it to the growers for $950 a month: two stories with terra cotta trim on Front and Davis streets, stores below, workers' flats and an assembly hall above, a large central arch on each street front leading to an open driveway, and one-story arcades of stalls on the sides.
Produce district businesses asked the Board of Works to replace the cobblestones in front of the Colombo Market with smooth bituminous paving that could be kept clean.
The earthquake and fires destroyed most of the Colombo Market along with the rest of the produce district.

The market was rebuilt on its old footprint from salvaged ruins, keeping the open drive aisle through arches on Front and Davis streets; most of the Front Street facade, including the surviving arch, dates from this reconstruction, and the second story was not rebuilt.
A banquet set on tables down the middle of Front Street, attended by the mayor, supervisors and 37 foreign consuls, celebrated the produce merchants for cleaning up the market streets.
A grand jury indicted seven directors of the Protective Society of Gardeners and Ranchers, headquartered in the Colombo Market, for conspiring to fix vegetable prices.
The District Attorney dismissed the 1910 price-fixing indictment against the Colombo Market growers' society.
A photograph shows the Front Street front reduced to the arch alone, with newer storefront windows and transoms in place of the other arches.
The Colombo Market raised its wholesale vegetable prices, setting off a dispute with the 1,400-member Retail Fruit Dealers Association, who turned to Sacramento Valley growers.
The Board of Supervisors designated the produce district, the Colombo Market included, a redevelopment area.
The Front operated here between 1959 and 1961, one of the North Beach bars and restaurants the city's survey identifies as significant in San Francisco's LGBTQ history.
Photographs show the arch still working as a market entrance, looking much as it had since 1906, shortly before the rest of the building came down.
Sasaki, Walker and Associates drew plans for a park on the Colombo Market site as part of the Golden Gateway redevelopment, keeping one structural bay of the market as a freestanding entrance arch.

The Redevelopment Agency demolished the Colombo Market and the surrounding produce district blocks for the Golden Gateway Center, sparing only the Front Street arch; the last produce merchants had moved out.
A newspaper caption described the old brick arch as salvaged as a memento of the produce district that once filled the site.
The Board of Supervisors adopted a resolution initiating landmark designation of the Colombo Market Arch.
The Historic Preservation Commission held a hearing and recommended the arch for landmark designation.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 311, Colombo Market Arch.
